title: Panic after a delivery
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on the labour ward. Grace, a midwife, tells you during a quiet moment that she has been having panic attacks since a traumatic delivery last month, in which a baby was born in poor condition.

She says she is coping at work but dreads her shifts. She asks you not to tell anyone.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Tell her to take time off work.
options.brief: Not your decision, and she says she is coping.
options.detailed: Time off may help some people, but she hasn't asked for it, and it isn't your decision.

options.text: Listen, and acknowledge how hard it has been.
options.brief: Feeling heard is important after trauma.
options.detailed: She has chosen to tell you. Listening without judgement helps her feel less alone.

options.text: Tell her that panic attacks are normal after a bad delivery.
options.detailed: Reactions like this are common, but saying they are 'normal' may make her feel she shouldn't seek help.

options.text: Tell the labour ward coordinator that she is struggling.
options.brief: Breaks her confidence without a safety reason.
options.detailed: She says she is coping and hasn't asked you to tell anyone. Sharing it without her agreement would damage trust.

options.text: Suggest she sees her GP about medication.
options.brief: Her GP may help, but medication isn't the first step.
options.detailed: Seeing her GP is reasonable, but suggesting medication as the answer is premature.

options.text: Encourage her to use the staff support service.
options.brief: Specialist support can help with trauma reactions.
options.detailed: Panic attacks after a traumatic event are common and treatable. Staff support services can help confidentially.

options.text: Avoid mentioning it again, so as not to upset her.
options.detailed: She opened up to you. Checking in later shows care.

options.text: Suggest she talks to a professional midwifery advocate.
options.brief: A source of support within midwifery.
options.detailed: Professional midwifery advocates offer restorative supervision and support after difficult events.

explanation.issue: This tests how you support a colleague after a traumatic event, respecting her confidence and pointing her to the right help.
explanation.keyDetails: She has panic attacks after a traumatic delivery. She is coping at work. She has asked for confidentiality.
explanation.reasoning: [B] listens, [F] points to staff support, and [H] suggests support within midwifery. The distractors overstep ([A], [D]), minimise ([C]), focus on medication ([E]), or withdraw ([G]).
explanation.competing: [E] is reasonable, as her GP can help. The problem is framing medication as the answer before support has been tried.

references.title: The Code: professional standards of practice and behaviour for nurses, midwives and nursing associates
references.note: Midwives' own wellbeing and access to support.
